---
title: "Between-participant designs"
---

Suppose an experiment asks whether multi-talker exposure supports recognition of a previously unheard talker with the same nonnative accent. Once a listener receives that exposure, the listener cannot return to the original unexposed state. Asking the same person to complete a control condition afterward would compare two moments in a learning process, not exposed and unexposed versions of the same initial listener.

In a [**between-participant design**](https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/), each participant contributes observations to only one condition. The condition effect is estimated by comparing groups rather than by subtracting two responses from the same participant. The resulting independence structure is the one used in the earlier chapter on [comparing two independent means](../statistical-inference/independent-means.qmd). This design preserves the meaning of a condition that has a lasting effect, though it also exposes the comparison to participant variation across groups.

## The comparison is across groups

Let $Y_i$ be one listener-level response, such as mean novel-talker keyword accuracy after exposure, and let $Z_i$ indicate the assigned condition. If $Z_i=1$ denotes multi-talker exposure and $Z_i=0$ denotes control exposure, the estimated group difference is

$$
\widehat\Delta=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0,
$$

where

$$
\bar Y_z=\frac{1}{n_z}\sum_{i:Z_i=z}Y_i.
$$

Each listener appears on only one side of this subtraction. Stable listener characteristics thus do not cancel within a difference score. Under the [random assignment mechanism](random-assignment.qmd), assignment is independent of potential responses by design, but realized groups can still differ by chance.

Now, you might wonder exactly what $\widehat\Delta$ targets. If we analyze listeners according to assignment, it estimates an intention-to-treat difference for the recruited listeners under the particular exposure, test talkers, sentences, and scoring rule. Generalization to new talkers or sentences requires those materials to be sampled and represented in the analysis; four hundred trials from the same fixed sentences do not establish that generalization.

## Working through a small comparison

Suppose four listeners receive multi-talker exposure and four receive control exposure. Their keyword recognition proportions are:

| listener | exposure | proportion correct |
|:--|:--|--:|
| P1 | multi-talker | .82 |
| P2 | multi-talker | .74 |
| P3 | multi-talker | .79 |
| P4 | multi-talker | .85 |
| P5 | control | .70 |
| P6 | control | .68 |
| P7 | control | .76 |
| P8 | control | .72 |

The multi-talker group mean is

$$
\bar Y_1=\frac{.82+.74+.79+.85}{4}=.80,
$$

and the control group mean is

$$
\bar Y_0=\frac{.70+.68+.76+.72}{4}=.715.
$$

Thus, the estimated difference is $.80-.715=.085$, or 8.5 percentage points. The estimate describes a behavioral performance contrast between the two realized groups. It does not, by itself, identify whether listeners changed acoustic-phonetic categories, attended to different cues, or adopted a different response strategy.

```{r}
recognition <- data.frame(
  listener = paste0("P", 1:8),
  exposure = rep(c("multi_talker", "control"), each = 4),
  proportion_correct = c(.82, .74, .79, .85, .70, .68, .76, .72)
)

group_means <- aggregate(
  proportion_correct ~ exposure,
  data = recognition,
  FUN = mean
)

group_means
with(recognition, t.test(
  proportion_correct[exposure == "multi_talker"],
  proportion_correct[exposure == "control"]
))
```

The two vectors passed to `t.test()` contain different participants, so the call does not use `paired = TRUE`. Treating the values as paired would invent a relation between P1 and P5, P2 and P6, and so on that the design never created.

## Trials improve measurement, not assignment replication

Each listener may complete many recognition trials. Those trials can make that listener's recognition proportion less sensitive to one unusually easy or difficult word. They do not replace additional independently assigned listeners when the target is a population difference between exposure conditions.

Suppose P1 completes 400 trials while every other listener completes 40. The study still contains eight independently assigned listeners. A trial-weighted mean would allow P1 to contribute ten times as much as another listener, which changes the target toward a randomly selected recorded trial. A listener-weighted mean gives each assigned listener one contribution, which matches a target over recruited listeners.

Sentences and test talkers can vary within listeners even when exposure varies only between listeners. The design record should thus state both that exposure is assigned between listeners and that keyword responses repeat within listeners, sentences, and possibly talkers. The earlier [mixed effects model sequence](../regression-models/structured-data.qmd) uses that record to represent shared variation.

## When this design is needed

Training, prolonged adaptation, and explicit instruction may have lasting effects. A between-participant design is appropriate when exposure to one condition changes how the listener would respond in another. It can also reduce demand effects when seeing multiple conditions would reveal the intended contrast.

The cost is that listener variation contributes directly to uncertainty. If a strong listener characteristic, such as baseline recognition on held-out materials, is measured before assignment, the restricted randomization procedure introduced on the previous page can balance condition counts within prespecified baseline groups. The same baseline measure should be retained in the analysis plan. This use is legitimate because the restriction is set before post-exposure outcomes are observed.

## Unpaired observations

A common failure is to arrange the two group vectors in some convenient order and run a paired analysis. The row positions then masquerade as pairs even though one participant has no natural counterpart in the other condition. The paired analysis usually understates uncertainty because it removes variation through an association that the design did not provide.

Another failure is to count trials as though condition were independently assigned to every trial. Both failures can be detected by writing the unit of assignment before writing the analysis.

::: {.callout-note title="Audit the between-participant comparison"}
1. Why does a lasting exposure manipulation favor a between-participant design?
2. Which observations appear on both sides of $\widehat\Delta$?
3. Why do 100 trials from one listener not count as 100 exposure assignments?
4. Under what condition may a baseline recognition measure be used to restrict assignment?
:::

A between-participant design compares groups whose members received only one condition. It protects manipulations that cannot be reset, while listener differences remain part of the group comparison. Within either participant structure, sentence versions must still be distributed so that item identity is not confused with condition. That is the role of [counterbalancing](counterbalancing.qmd).
